newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HKMA conference to highlight HK business as usual.
newsitem.headline: HKMA conference to highlight HK business as usual.

text.p: Hong Kong's financial sector hopes the hosting of a conference on Asian integration just 116 days before the territory reverts to China will send another signal that it will be business as usual after the handover.

"There is a huge perception out there that something big is going to happen, and it doesn't hurt to have people from the financial sector standing up and saying this is how we see things in Hong Kong," said Eric Nickerson, head of currency research and risk analysis at BA Asia.
Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.

Financial leaders will converge in Hong Kong on Friday to mull "the implications of increasing integration of financial markets in Asia and the role of Hong Kong in the years to come", said Joseph Yam, chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority.
The conference is jointly organised by HKMA, Hong Kong's de facto central bank, and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
"The meeting is a very appropriate channel to send out the message that Hong Kong will remain the same," said George Leung, economic adviser to Hongkong Bank.
"From an economist's viewpoint, the fundamentals, the procedures and rules that have been put in place and the trend of development still favor Hong Kong as a financial centre."

While political leaders from around the world have expressed concern about China's plan to dilute civil liberties in Hong Kong after the handover, international investors continue to eye Hong Kong and China credits favourably.
Local investors already are convinced, with polls showing that most Hong Kong people expect the economy to thrive after the handover.
"The environment certainly is right for Hong Kong to make some headway with foreign investors," said Nickerson.

The HKMA's Yam has taken to the road recently with his China counterparts to explain to investors the "one country, two systems" framework that will govern Hong Kong from July 1, and the role of the monetary authority.
Presentations have been made in Hong Kong, Tokyo and New York, and are scheduled for next week in Frankfurt.

At each venue, Yam has taken pains to explain to foreign investors that the authority will remain separate from China's central bank after July 1, and in fact will enjoy even more autonomy than under British colonial rule.
Yam has explained that the Hong Kong dollar will remain pegged to the U.S. dollar, and Hong Kong will remain in control of its fiscal policy.
People's Bank of China deputy governor Chen Yuan also has done his bit to assure the world that China has no intention of meddling in Hong Kong's financial affairs.
BA Asia's Nickerson was circumspect in his view.
"To highlight Hong Kong's role now probably does make sense because the outlook has turned positive, but does it make a difference?" Nickerson said.
"The reality still is that those people with big doubts will be looking to 1998, 1999 and 2000 to see how things have performed," he said.
